Chojnicki and Ragot [-@chojnicki2012] asked whether immigration could reduce the
fiscal burden of population ageing in France. Their answer, from a dynamic
general equilibrium model with overlapping generations, was yes, but modestly:
halting immigration in 2005 would have widened the social protection financing
gap by 1.3 points of GDP by 2050, while doubling net flows bought a smaller gain
than the demographic change it implied.

That paper calibrated its demographic block on the 2006 Insee projections. Insee
published a new projection exercise in June 2026. Both central assumptions have
moved sharply since, and in opposite directions.

| | Insee 2006 | Insee 2021 | Insee 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total fertility rate | about 1.9 | 1.80 | **1.45** from 2028 |
| Net migration, a year | about 100,000 | +70,000 | **+150,000** |

Observed fertility reached 1.56 in 2025, below the *low* variant of the 2021
exercise. Net migration reached 271,000 in 2022, above its *high* variant. The
natural balance turns negative from 2025, so population growth is now entirely
migratory.

This note does one thing: it recomputes the demographic ratio that drives the
pension side of the 2012 paper, using the 2026 projections, and compares it to
what that paper projected. It does not rebuild the general equilibrium model, so
nothing here speaks to GDP per capita, tax rates, or the financing gap itself.

## The dependency ratio under three migration scenarios

::: {.data-plate}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
dep = FileAttachment("data/dependency.csv").csv({typed: true})

viewof year = Inputs.range([2025, 2070], {
  value: 2050, step: 1, label: "Year", format: y => `${y}`
})

atYear = dep.filter(d => d.year === year)

Plot.plot({
  marginLeft: 46,
  marginRight: 150,
  height: 340,
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d", domain: [2000, 2070]},
  y: {label: "65 and over per 100 aged 15-64", grid: true, domain: [20, 65]},
  color: {legend: false},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([year], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.35}),
    Plot.line(dep, {x: "year", y: "ratio", stroke: "scenario", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(atYear, {x: "year", y: "ratio", fill: "scenario", r: 4}),
    Plot.text(atYear, {
      x: "year", y: "ratio", text: d => `${d.ratio.toFixed(1)}  ${d.scenario}`,
      dx: 8, textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 11
    }),
    Plot.ruleY([20])
  ]
})
```

:::

Source: Insee, 2026 population projections (Licence Ouverte 2.0). Ratio computed
from single years of age; it reproduces Insee's published aggregates to within
0.05 point. Insee's own published ratio uses 65+ over 20-64 and is not
comparable to the 65+ over 15-64 measure used here and in the 2012 paper.

## What the comparison gives

Chojnicki and Ragot projected a dependency ratio of 44.2 in 2050 under their
reference scenario, and 47.8 if immigration stopped in 2005. The 2026 central
projection, which assumes 150,000 net entries a year, gives **47.7 in 2050**.

Today's central case, with substantial immigration, sits where the 2012 paper
placed its zero-immigration counterfactual. The reason is not migration, which
runs above what that paper assumed, but fertility, which nobody assumed would
fall this far. The 2012 exercise treated immigration as one lever among several
against a demographic backdrop that has since deteriorated faster than the lever
can move it.

The spread across migration scenarios is also worth reading in magnitude rather
than in direction. Moving from 70,000 to 230,000 net entries a year — a range
of 160,000 people annually, sustained for forty-five years — shifts the 2050
ratio by 3.8 points, from 49.7 to 45.9. That is the same order as the 3.6-point
gap the 2012 paper found between its reference and no-immigration cases, and it
confirms their conclusion rather than overturning it: immigration moves the
dependency ratio, and it does not move it far.

## Who the immigrant population is

The 2012 paper's selective-immigration scenario turns on the skill composition
of entrants. That composition is worth looking at directly.

::: {.data-plate}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
qual = FileAttachment("data/qualification.csv").csv({typed: true})

sixOrder = [
  "No diploma or lower secondary",
  "Vocational certificate (CAP-BEP)",
  "Upper secondary (baccalaureat)",
  "Short-cycle tertiary (BTS, DUT)",
  "Bachelor's (licence, maitrise)",
  "Master's or doctorate"
]

viewof detail = Inputs.radio(["Six classes", "Three classes"], {
  value: "Six classes", label: "Detail"
})

qualRows = {
  const sel = qual.filter(d => d.age_min === 25);
  if (detail === "Six classes") {
    return sel.map(d => ({origin: d.origin, cls: d.qual, share: d.share}));
  }
  return d3.rollups(sel, v => d3.sum(v, d => d.share), d => d.origin, d => d.broad)
    .flatMap(([origin, a]) => a.map(([cls, share]) => ({origin, cls, share})));
}

Plot.plot({
  marginLeft: 200,
  marginRight: 20,
  height: detail === "Six classes" ? 260 : 150,
  x: {label: "Share of the population aged 25 and over (%)", grid: true},
  y: {label: null, domain: detail === "Six classes" ? sixOrder : ["Low", "Medium", "High"]},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(qualRows, {x: "share", y: "cls", fill: "origin", insetTop: 1.5, insetBottom: 1.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```

:::

Source: Insee, 2021 population census, detailed file (Licence Ouverte 2.0).
Immigrant follows the Insee definition: born a foreign national outside France.

The distribution is polarised rather than shifted. Immigrants aged 25 and over
are more often without a diploma than natives, by 16.8 points, and more often
holders of a master's degree or a doctorate, by 2.5 points. The deficit sits in
between, and it is largest on short-cycle tertiary degrees, at 5.7 points.

Part of the gap at the bottom measures where people were educated rather than
how much. The CAP-BEP is a French vocational credential that someone arriving as
an adult cannot hold, and foreign qualifications map poorly onto the French
nomenclature. Collapsing these six classes into the three used in the 2012 paper
hides the pattern entirely: the tertiary share then reads 31.0% for immigrants
against 34.4% for natives, a flat three-point deficit.

## Limits

The comparison with the 2012 figures is indicative, not exact. That paper's
demographic block came out of its own model, calibrated on 2006 projections, and
its text and its table give different age bounds for the dependency ratio. The
figures here are read against its published table.

Nothing in this note recomputes the fiscal side. The 2012 results on GDP per
capita, apparent tax rates and financing needs come from a general equilibrium
model that is not reproduced here, and the accounting decomposition of Chojnicki,
Ragot and Sokhna [-@chojnicki2022] would need per-capita contribution profiles by
age, origin and qualification that are published only as a figure.
